articles.title: In 2014, Savannah turned 160,000 cubic yards of dredged sediment into an 8-acre island that attracted more than 300 bird nests
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A patch of land built from material removed from a shipping channel became an unexpected nesting site for hundreds of birds in Savannah, Georgia. In M.
articles.body: A patch of land built from material removed from a shipping channel became an unexpected nesting site for hundreds of birds in Savannah, Georgia. In March 2014, the US Army Corps of Engineers completed an 8-acre island inside Savannah Harbor’s dredged material containment area 12A. Within its first nesting season, biologists had recorded more than 300 nests.The island was not created from untouched soil. Much of it was formed using sediment that had already been deposited during harbour dredging. Water was then pumped around the raised area, leaving a low, sandy island separated from the surrounding land. By late spring, black skimmers, black-necked stilts and several tern species were using the newly created ground.Savannah used 160,000 cubic yards of dredged sediment to build the bird islandThe island sits within one of seven containment areas used by the Savannah District to hold sediment removed from the federal shipping channel. Construction formed part of a wider project to raise and improve the site's dikes, rather than a standalone wildlife development.As reported by US Army Corps of Engineers, Savannah District, about 160,000 cubic yards of previously deposited dredged sediment were used to build the island. Another 877,000 cubic yards went towards raising the surrounding dike. The approach gave material already held at the site another use while creating an area suited to birds that nest on open ground.Construction of the wider project began in September 2012 and was completed in October 2013. The island was then impounded, with water pumped into the disposal area so that it surrounded the new nesting ground.36,000 cubic yards of sand gave the island a better nesting surfaceThe sediment did not form the island's entire surface. Engineers added 36,000 cubic yards of coarse sand moved from a nearby disposal area known as 14B. The sand was spread to a depth of about two feet. That surface was intended to remain relatively open, since dense vegetation can make bare-ground nesting areas less suitable for some shorebirds. Surrounding the island with water also made access more difficult for land-based predators, including feral hogs, coyotes and raccoons.That combination of exposed ground and isolation quickly became important during the first breeding season.More than 300 nests appeared in the first seasonBy May 30, 2014, Corps biologists had counted more than 300 nests on the new island. They included black skimmers, black-necked stilts, gull-billed terns and least terns. The least tern had particular significance for the monitoring work because it was listed as a threatened species in South Carolina at the time. The nesting area therefore served several species at once, rather than being designed around a single bird.During the April-to-August nesting period, biologists visited the harbour containment areas weekly. Their work involved counting birds and nests, checking for predators and watching to make sure sediment disposal activities did not disrupt nesting.The numbers could vary from day to day. Flocks of more than 1,000 birds were not unusual across the wider areas being monitored.Savannah’s bird islands also provide feeding and nesting habitatThe bird island formed part of the environmental mitigation associated with routine operation and maintenance of the Savannah Harbor Navigation Project. The Corps tracked bird populations and habitat use in the containment areas through annual reporting. The wider landscape also offered more than nesting space. Wetted sections of the containment areas provided thousands of acres of feeding habitat for waterfowl and shorebirds, while surrounding woodland supplied additional areas for feeding, roosting and nesting.By 2014, the Savannah District operated five interior bird islands, with two more being designed, as well as two near-shore islands.A dredged harbour site became a home for nesting birdsThe project illustrates how dredged sediment can become part of a constructed habitat rather than simply remaining a by-product of maintaining a navigation channel. In this case, material already deposited inside the containment area was reshaped into an island and then given a sandy surface suited to colonial water birds.The Corps also worked with state and federal agencies, including wildlife authorities in Georgia and South Carolina and the US Fish and Wildlife Service, as part of its monitoring and compliance work.For the birds using the site, the history of the material was less important than what was left on the surface: open sand, shallow water around the island and enough separation from many ground predators to provide a place to nest. In its first season, that was enough to produce more than 300 nests on a piece of ground that had been made from sediment removed during harbour maintenance.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump tells UN he has 'big decision' on whether to 'annihilate' Iran or make peace deal
articles.summary: His tone contrasted with remarks earlier from UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has told the United Nations General Assembly he faces a "big decision" on whether to strike Iran again or pursue a peace deal.

A single member of Iran's delegation watched on during the president's speech in New York, in which he said he could "annihilate" the Islamic Republic if the conflict went unresolved.

Before a standing-room-only audience, Trump also rejected "global government", vowed to broker peace between Russia and Ukraine and ensure the US wins the artificial intelligence race.

His tone contrasted with remarks earlier by UN Secretary General António Guterres, who warned global divisions were deepening and underscored the "interdependence" of the world's peoples.

Trump's speech on Tuesday came on a day of high-level diplomacy at the United Nations. He's meeting more than a dozen world leaders as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine test his foreign policy agenda.

He began by touting his accomplishments on the economy, immigration, the border and tackling violent crime, in remarks that sounded more pitched to voters in November's US midterm elections than the diplomats in Manhattan.

He spent much of his address justifying the war with Iran, which has spiked global oil prices while dragging down his approval ratings since the US and Israel launched the military action in February.

Trump argued that the conflict had prevented Tehran from obtaining a nuclear weapon and demonstrated the value of what he described as peace through strength - ultimatums rather than deal-making or compromise.

"Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?" he said.

"Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again? Do I drive them into hell?"

Trump said he believed an Iran deal, which has so far eluded him, would come right after November's elections.

The remarks were indicative of his foreign-policy strategy of coercive diplomacy - threatening overwhelming force while keeping negotiations open.

Trump later told reporters that American officials had had a "very productive" three-hour meeting with the Iranian delegation on the sidelines of the general assembly.

Iran state TV confirmed that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had met US Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, although there was no comment from officials in Tehran.

In his speech, Trump once again predicted his diplomacy would end Russia's war in Ukraine, which has shown little sign of letting up as the two sides trade tit-for-tat missile and drone strikes deep into each other's territory.

"We're working very closely with the leaders of Russia and Ukraine, and we will get that one done," Trump said. "It's going to happen, I think, more quickly than people understand."

Trump also played down fears about AI, vowing that the US would not surrender its lead to China because of alarmism or what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control the technology.

The US president argued artificial intelligence should instead be known as "super intelligence".

"The use of the word artificial makes it sound fake," he said. "It's not fake, it's actually amazing. But we have to be careful."

On the sidelines of the general assembly on Tuesday, Trump signed an agreement with the leaders of Denmark and Greenland to beef up US military presence on the North Atlantic island.

The deal reaffirms the sovereignty of Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, but grants the US broad access to the island's airspace and territory.

Trump is also meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and leaders from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman.

Earlier, Guterres gave his farewell speech as UN secretary general, urging unnamed superpowers to recognise "that their power isn't so super".

"The fault lines in our world are widening," Guterres said, citing geopolitical rivalries, wars, climate change and artificial intelligence.

By contrast, Trump criticised international institutions, accusing the UN of a "far-left agenda of globalist bureaucrats who nobody ever elected".

The US president instead emphasised national sovereignty and "unmatched" American military power.

"There is no global government," he said.

He also warned that the US would not allow threats to establish themselves anywhere in the Western hemisphere.

"If necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said.

Trump accused Cuba's communist government of cultivating ties to left-wing groups in the US, including the Communist Party USA, Antifa and the Democratic Socialists of America.

The Cuban delegation also appeared to walk out of the assembly chamber as Trump turned his sights on them, referring to the island as a "failed state".

articles.title: In the late 1980s, two explorers paddled the full length of the Amazon after walking its first 200 miles; they reached the Atlantic after a 4,200-mile journey
articles.summary: Rest of World News: In the late 1980s, Polish explorer Piotr Chmielinski and American writer Joe Kane became the first people to paddle the full length of the Amazon from.
articles.body: In the late 1980s, Polish explorer Piotr Chmielinski and American writer Joe Kane became the first people to paddle the full length of the Amazon from its source area to the Atlantic Ocean. Kane first walked 200 miles before joining the paddling journey. The expedition covered about 4,200 miles from the high-altitude headwaters to the sea and became a demanding test of endurance.The team faced dangerous rapids, altitude sickness, armed groups, difficult jungle conditions, and internal disputes. Only four of the original 11 members reached the Atlantic, and Kane and Chmielinski travelled nearly all of the river by boat, carrying their craft over land when the water became impossible to navigate.How Kane and Chmielinski travelled the Amazon by boatGuinness World Records identifies Piotr Chmielinski of Poland and Joe Kane of the United States as the first people to paddle the full length of the Amazon from its source area to the Atlantic. According to the record, the journey was completed in the late 1980s, with Kane walking the first 200 miles before joining the paddling expedition to Belem, Brazil. The explorers used kayaks for almost the entire route, switching to a raft for some of the rougher rapids. Other members of the expedition also joined them on the river. The expedition was the first to travel the length of the world’s longest river, covering about 4,200 miles from source to sea. Its account says Kane and Chmielinski travelled nearly the entire distance by boat.The long and difficult journey through the AndesThe journey began in the icy, high-altitude headwaters of the Amazon, where the 11-member team faced conditions that made the expedition difficult. The explorers included South Africans, Britons, Poles and Americans. They dealt with altitude sickness in the Andes and increasingly dangerous river rapids. In the eastern Andes, progress was especially slow.The expedition sometimes managed only 500 yards in a day despite long hours and serious risks. After three months, the group had travelled only 600 miles and was still in Peru. They still had 1,600 miles to cover before reaching Brazil and another 2,000 miles before the Atlantic. As per the Los Angeles Times, Kane and Chmielinski continued paddling, sometimes making 50 strokes a minute and 36,000 strokes a day, while navigating the waters.What threats and conflicts challenged the Amazon expeditionThe expedition became harder as the group faced new threats and disagreements grew within the team. The Los Angeles Times reported that the explorers encountered Maoist guerrillas at a bend in the river, were confronted by Peruvian soldiers downstream, and later came across armed cocaine traffickers.Personal rivalries eventually led to an open mutiny, reducing the original 11-member party to just four before the group reached the Atlantic. Kane and Chmielinski travelled nearly the entire Amazon by boat, carrying their craft over land whenever the river became too difficult to travel by boat. British doctor Kate Durrant and Polish photographer Zbyszek Bzdak also completed the journey, but they travelled much of the route by land while bringing supplies.Kane and Chmielinski reached the Atlantic after months of paddlingAfter months of difficult travel, Kane and Chmielinski finally reached the Atlantic Ocean, marking the end of their journey along the Amazon. When they reached the sea, they tasted the salt water and were soon taken to the United States after contacting a morning news programme from Belem. It also confirms that Kane walked the first 200 miles before joining the paddling journey.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'I tossed books across the room': Booker Prize judges reveal 'tussle' over shortlist
articles.summary: Past Booker winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are among the nominees for this year's award.
articles.body:
Past Booker Prize winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart have been shortlisted for the prestigious literary award again, after a selection process that the judges described as "a tussle".

Jamaican writer James is nominated this year for his latest novel The Disappearers; while Scottish author Stuart is shortlisted for John of John.

This year's other contenders are award-winning US novelist Elizabeth Strout, and British authors M John Harrison, Luke Kennard and Rebecca Perry.

But seven books that appeared on the longlist in July have been jettisoned, and Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the judging panel, said agreeing on the final six "has been, to put it mildly, hard work".

Scroll down to find out more about this year's nominees.

James previously won the Booker Prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, while Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain.

Praising this year's entries, Dame Mary added: "English language fiction now is full of talent – talent old and talent new.

"It's full of wit, seriousness, pleasure, challenge, discomfort and real brilliance, and I think we should be rewarding our novelists a lot more than we do."

The other judges included former Booker Prize-shortlisted US novelist Patricia Lockwood, who said she discovered she was "bossier than I believed myself to be" when making the case for or against particular books in the judges' meetings.

"I was sort of standing up a lot and tossing books across the room and being really active. I was like, 'Wow, yeah, I didn't know I had it in me'."

Another judge, poet Raymond Antrobus, told reporters: "All of us individually had a different idea for a shortlist and then it was a tussle."

Lockwood jokingly added: "A tussle, yeah. We wrestled like pigs in the mud!"

Antrobus said the final choices are connected because they are books that "as well as having heart, also took risk".

"These books, we truly believe, cannot be replicated by artificial intelligence. These are very human books for the way they talk about and navigate a lived experience."

The judging line-up was completed by journalist, editor and critic Rebecca Liu and Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, who said being on the selection panel was "a bit like being in a band".

He said: "The way a band makes an appealing noise is by everybody combining, in a way, and if you don't like that then you have to go solo.

"You get something that you couldn't get [alone] and no-one's in control of it and you make a good noise together. So I hope that's what this shortlist is, a nice noise."

Cocker read some of the entries while on tour, and said he joined one judges' meeting online while wearing a dressing gown in a hotel room in Australia at 02:00 local time.

"When you're on tour, it's quite dull when you're travelling so it was quite good to have something to read," he said.

"I became known for being in those meetings wearing a towelling robe."

The End of Everything by M John Harrison

An unexplained catastrophe, and the arrival of mysterious alien beings, have turned British society upside down - and a man and his elderly aunt muddle through on the Kent coast. It's the author's first Booker nomination, and he'd be the oldest ever winner at 81.

The judges said: "The End of Everything can be read as a thriller, a mystery, a satire, a dystopia, a road novel, a work of realism. The landscape may be bleak, the catastrophe may be immersive, yet there still were moments we found ourselves laughing aloud."

This epic, visceral story revolves around a violent attack on eight gay men who had gathered to rehearse a queer play in Kingston, Jamaica, in 1988, and its aftermath. The New York Times called it "a masterpiece, the novel of the decade and possibly of the century thus far".

The judges said: "A Jamaican epic from one of the most impactful Caribbean novelists today; readers will love the shifting register of the dialogue and poetic phrasings, often pierced through with sharp, double-edged humour."

An out-of work actor gets a new role - being locked in a black bag during psychology lectures for an entire term as a professor's experiment. The story unfolds into a humorous and poignant satire that makes sharp observations about the state of modern masculinity and creative life.

The judges said: "In a wonderfully quirky campus novel, Kennard combines an absurd experiment with a moving story about human frailty, passion, confusion and identity. There's something for everyone here."

A modern-day museum curator is commissioned to recreate a past scene in a historic palace, and becomes immersed in the world of the young, reluctant king whose life she uncovers. It is the debut novel by Perry, who is also a poet and a former competitive trampolinist.

The judges said: "An affecting and lush jewel of a novel that moves between our present-day world to a medieval court and unsettles the idea that there's ever one universal historical truth."

The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout

Strout, a former Pulitzer Prize winner and double Booker nominee, tells the story of a high school history teacher in his 50s who feels adrift in modern America. When a secret emerges, he must face big questions about his relationships and life choices.

The judges said: "A novel that engages with the deeply divisive politics of present-day America, without itself becoming divisive. This is the kind of book we need now: a calm antidote to contemporary events."

The third novel by Stuart is about a fashion student who is drawn back to his home in a small, religious community in the Outer Hebrides in the mid-1990s. He and his father both nurse secrets. And both are called John.

The judges said: "A rich and moving novel about a father and son who live on a remote Scottish island in the 1990s, where small-town secrets and buried shame reverberate to surprising, devastating and even joyous effect."

The winner will receive £50,000 and will be announced in London on 9 November. The ceremony will be broadcast live on a special edition of BBC Radio 4's Front Row.

Longlisted books that did not make the final cut included Emma Cline's Switzy, which had been seen by some as a frontrunner for the prize.

"Believe me, this is a nailed-on Booker winner," critic Giles Coren wrote in the Times this weekend.

"If this one doesn't win, I'll eat Mary Beard."

Dame Mary responded on Tuesday: "I know Giles Coren said he wants to eat me if Switzy isn't on the shortlist.

"Well, I'm going to get the cooker prepared and ask him how he wants me done."

articles.title: Ukraine anger as EU removes Russian oligarchs from sanctions list
articles.summary: Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman both have close ties to President Putin, and Kyiv said the move sent Moscow the wrong signals.
articles.body:
The European Union is to remove sanctions on two oligarchs imposed after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to reports, prompting anger in Ukraine.

France had campaigned for Russian-Uzbek billionaire Alisher Usmanov to be taken off the list, citing "national security concerns". Luxembourg called for the removal of Russian-Israeli businessman Mikhail Fridman, who is suing the country for the release of frozen assets.

Latvia initially opposed the deal but agreed to a compromise, part of which involved extending sanctions on nearly 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years.

Ukrainian officials said the move was "unacceptable" and sent the wrong signal to Moscow.

"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.

He urged all EU member states to instead announce national sanctions on the two individuals. Latvia has already said it would do so.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov earlier welcomed the prospect of the two oligarchs being taken off the list, claiming the EU's sanctions were illegal and all Russians should be removed.

Usmanov founded USM Holding company , an investment group that owns iron, steel and copper suppliers, and the Megafon telecommunications company. He has in the past had ties with the English Premier League clubs Arsenal and Everton.

The EU froze his assets in 2022, describing him as "a pro-Kremlin oligarch with particularly close ties to Russian president Vladimir Putin". Usmanov said the decision was "unfair".

It has been reported that France's initiative was linked to a prospective prisoner release deal with Azerbaijan.

Fridman, a Russian-Israeli citizen born in Ukraine, is the founder of the Alfa Group investment conglomerate, with key interests in energy and banking. The EU has described him as a top Russian financier and enabler of Putin's inner circle.

Fridman himself said at the time of Russia's full-scale invasion that the conflict should end as soon as possible , but avoided outright condemnation of President Putin.

His Russian-Latvian business partner Pyotr Aven was stripped of Latvia's highest civilian honour in 2022 for failing to condemn the invasion of Ukraine.

This may have influenced Latvia's opposition to the move, vetoing it in a vote by EU ambassadors on Monday.

However, on Tuesday it changed its vote to an abstention as a compromise was reached. The new deal involved extending sanctions on some remaining 2,600 individuals and entities to three years. Until now, sanctions had to be renewed every six months.

Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also announced that France had agreed to start talks with Latvia about joining a French nuclear deterrence initiative and strengthen its military presence in Latvia.

articles.title: In 2017, June Thomas started rescuing ‘rez dogs’ from her home in Manitoba; after surveying 200 homes and helping sterilise 65+ animals, she has now opened an on-reserve shelter
articles.summary: US News: In 2017, June Thomas began rescuing stray “rez dogs” from her own home on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation in southern Manitoba, driven by concern.
articles.body: In 2017, June Thomas began rescuing stray “rez dogs” from her own home on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation in southern Manitoba, driven by concern for the many unvaccinated, unsterilised animals roaming the reserve. After surveying 200 homes, helping sterilise more than 65 dogs and cats and coordinating several on-reserve clinics, she has now opened what she believes is Manitoba’s first on-reserve animal shelter. The facility, run under her organisation Ginew Animal Care Services, aims to provide a sustainable, community-led solution to overpopulation and disease while reducing the need to transport pets off-reserve for basic care, according to IndigiNews.From a personal loss to a community missionJune Thomas’s journey began with grief. Her beloved dog Bessie fell ill and died from canine parvovirus, a highly contagious and often fatal disease that spreads quickly among unvaccinated dogs. Watching Bessie suffer made Thomas realise how vulnerable animals were in her community, where access to routine veterinary care, vaccinations and spay-and-neuter services was limited. What started as a small home-based effort she called “June’s Adoptables” gradually grew as more dogs and cats needed help.Over time, the operation outgrew her house. Thomas enrolled in a veterinary assistant program, graduating in 2024 from Robertson College and becoming certified to administer vaccinations. That training gave her the confidence and skills to formalise her work. She incorporated as Ginew Animal Care Services and began planning a dedicated shelter on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation, about 100 kilometres south of Winnipeg. In February 2026, the shelter opened its doors, marking a major milestone in her nearly decade-long effort.Understanding “rez dogs” and the challenges they faceOn many First Nations reserves, “rez dogs” are mixed-breed strays that roam freely without a single owner. They are often treated as community animals, fed by different households and allowed to move between properties. For many residents, these dogs are seen as relatives rather than pets in the conventional sense. Yet this informal system can create problems when animals are not vaccinated, sterilised or monitored for illness.Uncontrolled breeding leads to rapid population growth. Puppies are born faster than homes can be found for them. Diseases like parvo can spread through packs, especially among young dogs with weak immune systems. In some cases, large groups of stray dogs can become a safety concern, particularly if they form packs and behave aggressively toward people. Advocates stress that these issues are not a sign that community members do not care about animals, but rather a reflection of limited infrastructure and veterinary resources on reserves.Door-to-door surveys and sterilisation clinicsThomas took a methodical approach to addressing overpopulation. With support from band council, she helped develop an animal bylaw and management plan for Roseau River in 2021. Once the plan was ratified, she went door to door, surveying roughly 200 homes to ask whether residents had dogs or cats, whether they wanted to register them and whether the animals had been vaccinated or sterilised. This groundwork gave her a clear picture of how many animals needed care and where the biggest gaps were, as per the report.At first, she met resistance. Many people did not understand why spaying and neutering mattered, or why vaccinations were important. Some were unsure where to take sick animals or how much care would cost. Thomas responded by organising on-reserve spay-and-neuter clinics, removing the barrier of having to travel to veterinarians outside the community. The first clinic cost more than $15,000, with six different community programs chipping in to cover the bill.Those clinics made a tangible difference. More than 65 dogs and cats were sterilised, and 32 animals were rescued from the reserve. Attendance at later clinics showed the impact. A spay-and-neuter event on July 1 drew about 30 sign-ups. Just two weeks later, Thomas struggled to find 10 or 15 animals that still needed the procedure, not because interest had faded but because many pets were already up to date on shots and sterilised. Revisiting her original survey data, Thomas saw the overall dog and cat population drop from 214 registered animals to an estimated 117, thanks to sterilisation, surrenders and rescues. She also noted that parvo had not been seen in the community for about a year, which she credits to public education and regular clinics.Building the shelter with band revenuesThe new shelter represents the next phase of Thomas’s vision. Roseau River’s chief and council funded the construction using revenues from land leases and tobacco sales tax, according to Thomas. The facility includes space for housing animals, areas for cleaning and feeding, and plans for a dedicated water system. Thomas and other volunteers work at the shelter six to eight hours a day, cleaning, hauling water, transporting animals and providing food and basic care. None of them draw a salary, and fundraising to keep Ginew Animal Care running is constant.Since the grand opening, Thomas has received calls and messages from other First Nations interested in replicating the model. Her advice is simple. Involve the community from the start. If people feel ownership over the project, they will support it. She acknowledges that reserves need more help advocating for animals and securing stable funding, but she also believes that solutions must come from within communities rather than being imposed from outside.The wider picture of infrastructure gapsThomas’s work sits within a broader context of underfunded infrastructure on First Nations reserves. Former veterinarian Richard Herbert describes stray dog issues as a symptom of larger systemic gaps, including shortages of quality housing, limited medical services, unreliable clean water and poor access to affordable food. In his view, animal management cannot be separated from these foundational issues. He urges non-Indigenous animal advocates to “stop the shame game” and recognise that the problem is not a lack of care but a lack of resources.Data on dog-related injuries and deaths in Indigenous communities is sparse. Neither Statistics Canada nor Health Canada routinely compiles national statistics that distinguish First Nations and Inuit communities from the rest of the population. Herbert’s own review of CBC News archives from 1998 to 2007 found 11 dog-mauling deaths of children under eight, seven of which occurred in First Nations and Inuit communities. Based on 2001 Census data, he estimated that First Nations children were 180 times more likely to be killed by a dog than other children in Canada, though he stresses this is an estimate, not an official statistic.Sovereign solutions, not savioursAdvocates like Alexandra Jarrett of Save Rez Dogs emphasise a “sovereign” approach to animal welfare. Rather than framing First Nations members as incompetent pet owners, she argues for compassion toward relatives who lack the resources to care for their animals at a given time. Save Rez Dogs avoids language like “rescue” that can carry colonial overtones, and instead supports community-led strategies that respect how dogs are viewed locally. In many Indigenous communities, dogs have traditionally served roles such as protecting against bears or pulling sleds, and any management plan should begin by understanding those roles.Herbert suggests permanent veterinary facilities on reserves, similar to nursing stations, where routine procedures could be performed without flying or driving animals long distances. He also highlights the need for animal control officers, shelters, education programs and enforcement mechanisms to make bylaws effective. Without this broader infrastructure, even well-intentioned plans can falter.A model others can adaptRoseau River’s shelter is still in its early days and does not yet have a permanent funding source. Indigenous Services Canada has not established dedicated on-reserve animal welfare programs, though pilot projects like Matawa First Nations Management Animal Services are being watched as possible models. Provincial programs in Manitoba fund some mobile veterinary and spay-and-neuter clinics, but reserves fall under federal jurisdiction, creating gaps in responsibility and financing.Despite these challenges, Thomas’s work offers a practical blueprint. Combine door-to-door engagement with accessible sterilisation and vaccination services. Build community ownership through education and involvement. Use band revenues where possible while advocating for longer-term support. Encourage Indigenous youth to pursue veterinary careers, as two of her volunteers are now planning to do. For Thomas, the shelter is not just about animals. It is about strengthening community capacity, reducing suffering and showing that Indigenous-led solutions can address problems that have long been ignored.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2020, ExxonMobil toppled the 27,000-ton Lena platform 50 miles off Louisiana, turning the 1,078-foot oil structure into an artificial reef site
articles.summary: US News: In a groundbreaking move, ExxonMobil has transformed the 27,000-ton Lena platform into an artificial reef off the coast of Louisiana, promoting marine life and sustainability through the Rigs-to-Reefs Program.
articles.body: On July 3, 2020, ExxonMobil's Lena Compliant Tower jacket was toppled in place about 50 miles southeast of Grand Isle, Louisiana, converting the 1,078-foot structure into a deepwater artificial reef. Installed in 1983 as the Gulf's first cable-stabilized platform, Lena operated for more than three decades before decommissioning. According to the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement, it became the tallest oil and gas platform in the Gulf of Mexico ever converted into a reef under the Rigs-to-Reefs Program.The Lena was installed in 1983 as the Gulf's first cable-stabilized platformThe Lena Compliant Tower was constructed in 1983 at Mississippi Canyon Block 280 at depths of about 1,000 feet, and became famous as the first cable-stabilized, or guyed, production platform ever to be erected in the Gulf of Mexico region. The jacket of the platform itself stood at an elevation of 1,078 feet and weighed 27,000 tons, while including the platforms and drilling rig, it stretched to 1,300 feet, about 50 feet higher than the Empire State Building's roofline of 1,250 feet, not counting its spire, according to Offshore Magazine and BSEE (2020). It remained a productive well for 33 years and stopped producing in 2016.BSEE approved the reefing after years of coordination with LouisianaThe conversion was done through the Rigs-to-Reefs Program, which is administered by the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement (BSEE), an agency of the United States government that regulates energy operations at sea. Per BSEE, approval for the removal of the platform was given by the bureau after consideration, after several years of cooperation by the bureau, ExxonMobil, and the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries over the issue of the removal and reefing of the platform. Then, BSEE director Scott Angelle said the project showed how industry and government can cooperate to preserve the marine environment of the Gulf region.The jacket was toppled in place on July 3, 2020Instead of towing the Lena offshore or dismantling it at the shore, the jacket structure of the Lena was disconnected from its original mooring and was deliberately toppled right at its current location on July 3, 2020, forming a reef on the Gulf of Mexico's outer continental shelf. According to Keith Matocha, the decommissioning project manager of ExxonMobil, the aim was to maintain the structure's ability to support life because the formation of a reef would mean that the rare deep-water corals of the Gulf of Mexico would still survive, along with encrusting organisms, which would then attract other marine life.Louisiana is expected to take over ownership once the site is clearedAs of the 2020 announcement, ownership of the Lena jacket was expected to transfer to the Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries once the site was surveyed and cleared, a process officials anticipated completing in early 2021. Current sourcing does not confirm whether that transfer has since taken place. The Louisiana Department of Wildlife and Fisheries was supposed to handle the site, which is one of the sites included by Louisiana in the Rigs-to-Reefs program that allows states to take control of jackets instead of removal.The Lena reefing was part of a long-running Gulf of Mexico program. In the Gulf alone, the BSEE has given its approval to more than 500 Rigs-to-Reefs initiatives since the launch of the program in 1987, of which 47 approvals were done just in the three years before the Lena reefing. U.S. Congressman Garret Graves, whose constituency is Grand Isle, called the program a method of making a decommissioning liability an asset.From production platform to permanent reef habitatNearly four decades after installation, the Lena's subsea structure now serves a different role underwater in the Gulf. The jacket was not taken out once its service life for oil and gas production came to an end but has been left there as an artificial reef site, one of the biggest examples converted by the Gulf of Mexico's Rigs-to-Reefs Program so far.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Lib Dems leave conference buoyed by Davey's message
articles.summary: Concerns over Sir Ed Davey's leadership were dampened by pledges at conference and his performance.
articles.body:
This was a more sombre, more serious, Sir Ed Davey.

The stunts - from falling off paddleboards to hurtling down rollercoasters – were scaled back at this year's Liberal Democrat party conference.

"This is the fight of our lives," he repeatedly told his party. The focus, much like his conference speech last year, was on Reform UK.

But the announcement he'd held back for his speech was aimed at Conservative-leaning voters: tax cuts worth billions.

And not just for lower income earners, but for those in the higher 40% rate of tax too.

Part of the announcement – raising the amount you can earn before you pay income tax altogether – was the same policy Davey's bête noire, Reform UK, announced at their conference a couple of weeks ago.

The dividing line he drew was over how it was paid for. Nigel Farage's party would reduce spending on benefits to fund the tax cut.

The Lib Dem leader said he would pay for it through the economic growth he believes could be gained by rejoining the EU's Single Market and a customs union.

Lib Dems vow to end 'computer says no' economy to boost growth

Lib Dems call for one-to-one midwife care during childbirth

Davey promises tax cuts for millions if UK rejoins EU single market

By putting the European Union at the heart of how he would fund his tax cut, the Lib Dems couldn't be drawing a starker contrast with the Brexit-backing Reform UK and a Conservative Party also committed to cutting welfare.

But the plan is speculative. The Lib Dems insist a deal with the EU could be negotiated within a year if the party was in government after the next election.

Plenty of economic experts, including the official budget forecaster the OBR, believe the UK's economy could grow if the UK was in the Single Market.

But as recent political history teaches us, negotiating a deal with the European Union is often more difficult than party leaders hope.

And basing a tax cut on potential future economic growth is a risky business.

There is also uncertainty over whether the Lib Dems' sums add up. The independent think tank, the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the policy as set out in the press release would cost "much more" than the £17bn the Lib Dems have budgeted for.

The party says the tax cut wouldn't come in until the fifth year after the next election. So even if the party got into power and successfully negotiated an EU deal, the tax cut could be eight years away.

But the Lib Dem MPs I spoke to afterwards were less focused on these details than the message it sent to voters.

Davey came into this conference facing criticism over his leadership from some MPs in private and others in his party in public worrying about the party's ambition and direction.

For now those concerns have been dampened. "That was the speech a lot of us have been waiting for him to give," one Davey-sceptic MP told me afterwards.

A small number are uncomfortable with the main policy from the party's conference being a tax cut that would most benefit the better off.

One told me they would rather the focus had been wooing younger voters by tackling the amount graduates repay in student loans, an old bruise for the Lib Dems.

But overall this speech, and this conference, was well received by the Lib Dem faithful.

They are a party honing their messaging before the next general election. The strategy is primarily on those 27 seats where the Lib Dems came second in 2024. Most of them are held by the Conservatives and Davey's tax cuts are aimed at appealing to those voters.

But already the attack from the Tories has been that the Lib Dems are "Labour's lapdog". That attack is in part because Davey has given his most explicit answer this week on not going into a coalition government with the Conservatives after the next general election. He's done the same for Reform UK.

But he hasn't ruled out a pact with Labour.

So that attack from the Conservatives will come again and again before the next election.

But the Lib Dems leave their Brighton conference buoyed, with sights not just on retaining their record 72 seats won at the last election, but on winning some more.

"I've got no ceiling on our ambitions," Davey said this week.

He has already served in government once, in coalition with David Cameron's Conservatives. His eyes are on another stint in office.

articles.title: Kristi Noem takes heat after bagging a massive elk & Keely Hodgkinson's sexy new speedsuit is a talker
articles.summary: Kristi Noem bags a massive elk on a Wyoming archery hunt and fires back at online critics, while Keely Hodgkinson debuts Nike's new speedsuit.
articles.body: 'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com. We did it, friends. We made it to fall. Now, I know Joe Kinsey tried to convince you in this morning's Screencaps that preferring autumn to summer is some sort of psy-op. That pumpkin spice is the devil's cocaine. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE But, respectfully, that just sounds like the opinion of someone who lives in northern Ohio. For those of us suffering in the ungodly heat and 400% humidity of the American South, sweater weather can't come soon enough. In fact, today is the first time in nearly a month (26 days) that the temperature hasn't surpassed 90 degrees. I mean, it's still 85. But baby steps. Fun fact: just last week, the largest heat dome on planet Earth was centered right over my home state of Tennessee. I'll let this guy tell you all about it: In other words, it's been miserable. Man, I'm doing so much whining you'd think I was Caleb Williams pulling a hamstring. Point is, I am positively giddy about dropping temperatures, changing leaves, fall hiking and not drowning in a vat of my own sweat. Hell, I might even burn a pumpkin candle — just to get all the haters riled up. Speaking of haters, welcome to Tuesday Nightcaps, where Kristi Noem is taking some online heat for killing an animal. (Not her dog this time, thank God.) But first, we're talking running fashion. Buckle in, kids, and let's do this thing. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Keely Hodgkinson debuts sexy new speedsuit Keely Hodgkinson — an Olympic middle distance runner for Team Great Britain, in case you didn't know — turned some heads at the season-ending Athlos meet in North London on Friday. That's because, while all the other runners were decked out in their standard tiny bottoms and tanks, Keely rolled up in an all black, full-body catsuit. Excuse me, it's a "zero-distraction speed suit," according to Nike. But, respectfully, it was a little distracting. Just check out the aerodynamics on that thing! I personally feel a little vindicated by Keely's look. In the handful of distance races I've done, the "serious" runners always say to me, "How do you run in leggings?!" As if I might as well tape concrete blocks to my feet while I'm at it. And my answer is always the same: how do you NOT run in leggings? See, the way my thighs are set up, running long distance in a pair of shorty shorts would just mean punching a one-way ticket to Chafe-town. Granted, I'm just a casual neighborhood runner — not an Olympic sprinter. So what do I know? This reminds me of that time a couple of years ago when Nike debuted its Team USA track and field kits for the Paris Olympics. The internet freaked out over the "sexist" designs meant to sexualize female track and field athletes instead of equipping them with comfortable and appropriate attire to compete. Turns out, though, what actually happened is that Nike offered the women about 20 different combinations of a uniform — with tops and bottoms of various lengths. The ladies even had the option of wearing the men's kit if it would make them more comfortable. It just so happens, though, that nearly all the female athletes chose to wear the tiny bikini and sports bra combo. So the outrage was entirely overblown. As social media outrage tends to be. I digress. Keely is having none of those front-wedgie-inducing underwears. And I don't blame her one bit. She won the women's 800-meter event wearing that catsuit, by the way. So she might be onto something. Kristi Noem bags a massive elk It's been a rough year for ol' Kristi Noem. First, she was ousted from her role as DHS Secretary. And then came those um... unflattering photos of her husband. Kristi got knocked down. But in the spirit of Chumbawamba, she got up again. And now, she's bagged a massive elk on an archery hunting trip in Wyoming. I can't show you the picture of her and the actual elk because Instagram has deemed it too graphic for embeds. But you can see the gigantic animal she harvested here if you're interested. EVA SHOCKEY SAYS WOMEN DON'T HAVE TO ABANDON THEIR FEMININITY TO BELONG IN THE OUTDOORS You really have to toe the line with hunting content on Instagram. You can post all the dead fish photos you want, but as soon as you show a mammal down, it becomes a whole thing. Last week, I posted a cute little video of NASCAR driver Chase Briscoe talking about his 4-year-old son's love of hunting on OutKick OutDoors. Instagram finally allowed it, but it got shadow banned on YouTube and removed from TikTok for "violating community guidelines." Annoying. Predictably, Kristi has gotten plenty of hate in the comments for harvesting this big, beautiful bull elk. And yes, probably from the same people who have no problem grabbing a Big Mac from the McDonald's drive-thru. Because as long as you don't have to actually see the dead animal you're eating, you can delude yourself into believing you have the moral high ground. Kristi put the critics in their place, calling them "ignorant and uninformed." "Of course this beautiful animal will nourish our family and many others we will share with," she wrote. "These majestic animals are incredible and I’ve so loved learning their ways from my father, sharing memories in the mountains with him and my brothers and now my friends." Kristi concluded: "Shame on you who desecrate and don’t understand the stewardship responsibilities God has given us. Go to a store and shop for anything that hasn’t been harvested and you will find bare shelves and your family will starve." Anyway, who wants elk burgers? Let's open the mailbag. 📩 Email: amber.harding@outkick.com (Send your thoughts, stories, tips, rants and photos of your dog.) 🐦 Twitter/X: @TheAmberHarding 📸 Instagram: @amberharding Readers support outdoorswoman Ella Langley Last week, we talked about how some losers (unsuccessfully) tried to cancel Ella Langley after some old photos resurfaced of her deer hunting in Alabama. Gary B. writes: The state of NJ has such an over population of deer that the hunting season has been extended. They are destroying the ecosystem. The season starts October 3rd and me and my brother are tracking a massive buck on his property in the southern Pine Barrens. His son got a large buck last year and hopefully that trend will continue. As far as the WNBA, basketball in general sucks. The game went south when they added the 3 point line. Basketball used to almost be as physical as football or hockey. You had to control the paint it was an inside game of strength. Now they shoot soon as they cross the half court line. The only basketball I watch is college hoops in the month of March. That's awesome but then again college sports are in my opinion better then the professional level mainly because of the intensity of the crowd . Texas and Ohio State proves my point. Nikki S. writes: Love Ella and all the hate only shows she’s "made it." Unfortunately that’s the world we live in today. And btw pretty sure the majority of Ella’s fan base was raised where hunting and fishing were both recreation and a source of food. Steve B. writes: The idiot who thinks hunting is a moral problem, has never gone to a slaughterhouse or feedlot to see how his porterhouse steak is actually created. Miami Dolphins fans unite in misery John G. writes: I have the pain and joy of watching this teams since founding when Wilson was the coach and his son was the QB. Been thru the the perfect season. Also attended their first game in now named Hard Rock stadium when the team was owned by the "Garbage Man". So I have seen the highlights and low lights. They will be back maybe not this year but eventually. I just hope they don't capture Detroit's record. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Amber: Listen, if you're gonna tank, TANK. None of this 6-11, 5-12 crap. I'm expecting a full buy-in from team personnel: No. 1 draft pick or bust, baby. One more thing: gorilla gets a wellness check If you've never seen a massive silverback gorilla have a medical checkup, now you have. articles.title: Federal judge temporarily blocks deportation of illegal immigrant shot by ICE officer in Austin, attorney says
articles.summary: A federal judge has reportedly blocked the deportation of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, who was shot by ICE in Austin during a Sunday confrontation.
articles.body: A federal judge has blocked the deportation of an illegal immigrant shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Austin over the weekend, his attorney said. Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, who represents him, said her office has filed a federal lawsuit on behalf of her client, 28-year-old Wilber Rafael Garces Perez. A judge ordered that Perez be present for a Sept. 30 hearing. "That means Wilber cannot be deported in the meantime," Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote on Facebook. "For now, we have secured a temporary block on his deportation while his case moves forward." SOCIALIST, COMMUNIST GROUPS COORDINATE, PROMOTE 'SPONTANEOUS' ANTI-ICE PROTESTS IN AUSTIN She added that Perez still requires medical care and "we will continue fighting to protect his rights." He is still in "a lot of pain" and the bullet that struck him is still lodged in his body, she said. Perez, a Venezuelan citizen, was delivering a DoorDash order when he made a U-turn under the highway before ICE agents continued to pursue him. BRANDON GILL UNLOADS ON DEMOCRATS OVER ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHARGED WITH RAPING TEEN: 'COLLATERAL DAMAGE' "The truck chased him and sideswiped him again. And the agents came out and shot him in the back of the neck and pulled him out of the car," Lincoln-Goldfinch said. Perez had a final order of removal, authorities said. However, Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client received a removal order after a notice for his immigration hearing was sent to his old address, despite him having updated his address with the court. FEDERAL APPEALS COURT COMPARES TRUMP MIGRANT DETENTION POLICY TO JAPANESE AMERICAN INTERNMENT Travis County District Attorney Jose Garza sent a letter Tuesday to Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin and ICE Director David Venturella asking that Garces Perez be allowed to remain in the United States pending an investigation into the shooting. Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, and more than 100 other members of Congress also signed a letter to Mullin and Venturella demanding that Perez be released from ICE detention so he can receive medical treatment. ICE OFFICER PLEADS NOT GUILTY TO LYING ABOUT MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING INVOLVING VENEZUELAN MAN The lawmakers also asked that state authorities and law enforcement preserve all evidence from the shooting. "Mr. Garces Perez is a key witness to this shooting, and given ICE's history of obscuring the facts in similar investigations, he must not be removed," the letter said. DOJ CHARGES ICE OFFICER WITH LYING TO INVESTIGATORS FOLLOWING MINNEAPOLIS SHOOTING OF VENEZUELAN MAN The ICE officer who shot Perez is a new recruit to the agency but has years of law enforcement experience, including with the U.S. Border Patrol, sources told Fox News. In addition, that unidentified officer wasn't wearing a body camera at the time of the shooting, multiple federal law enforcement sources told Fox News. ICE is supposed to have every officer equipped with cameras by the end of the month. The officer completed the agency’s 256-hour Deportation Officer Training Program in August 2025 before undergoing additional operational and legal instruction through 2026, records show. According to training logs, the officer scored 99.2% on his pistol qualification and completed coursework on use-of-force scenarios, as well as less-lethal tactics involving Tasers, OC spray, and batons. His curriculum also included field operations training and practical exercises covering the entire custody continuum, alongside instruction on warrantless arrests, Title 19 authority, escort and removal procedures, expedited removal and custody procedures. ICE AGENTS IN FATAL HOUSTON SHOOTING WERE NOT WEARING BODY CAMERAS, SOURCES SAY Fox News Digital has reached out to ICE and the Department of Homeland Security. In the wake of the shooting, multiple Democrats have criticized ICE, calling it a "rogue" agency that was "terrorizing our cities and threatening the safety of our residents." Meanwhile, on Tuesday, DHS released a list of some illegal immigrants in Texas who have been arrested for various crimes, including supporting an Islamic State-inspired mass shooting on election day in 2024 and two Mexican citizens wanted for multiple murders in their native country. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The list also includes child sex offenders, drug dealers, and one Mexican man arrested after posting a TikTok video in 2025 in Spanish soliciting the murder of ICE agents and offering a $10,000 reward.

articles.title: Trump admin asks top US court to reverse pro-Palestinian scholar’s release
articles.summary: US solicitor general challenges lower court’s ruling on Georgetown scholar’s detention, sparking constitutional debates.
articles.body:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump has asked the US Supreme Court to overturn the decision to release a Georgetown University scholar who had advocated for Palestinian rights and opposed Israel’s war in Gaza.

Georgetown scholar and postdoctoral fellow Badar Khan Suri was released last year after a judge heard claims that his detention violated his due process and free speech rights under the US Constitution.

On Monday, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) petitioned the high court to consider whether federal immigration law barred the lower-court judge from ordering Suri’s release.

Suri, an Indian citizen, was first arrested by masked US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers outside his home in Rosslyn, Virginia, in March 2025 amid the Trump administration’s targeted crackdown and mass deportation campaigns of foreign nationals and visa holders engaged in pro-Palestinian activism across college ‌campuses.

At the time, critics accused the Trump administration of targeting him based on his familial ties. His wife is the daughter of Ahmed Yousef, a former adviser to assassinated Hamas political leader Ismail Haniyeh.

Suri was brought to Texas after his detention and freed in May 2025 on the orders of a district court judge, on the grounds that he was likely to succeed in proving his arrest was in retaliation for his constitutionally protected speech.

The Trump administration has argued that the judge should not have interfered in the case.

In July , the Virginia-based US Circuit Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit ruled in a 2-1 decision that nothing prevented a lower-court judge from hearing a challenge to someone’s allegedly unconstitutional detention, even if it related to deportation proceedings pending before the immigration courts.

Solicitor General D John Sauer argued that the Fourth Circuit’s ruling threatened nationwide immigration enforcement by letting detainees bypass immigration courts to contest their deportations.

“That is all practically ⁠disastrous,” Sauer said.

Sauer noted that a different appeals court had reached the opposite conclusion earlier this year, overturning a ruling that freed pro-Palestinian activist and former Columbia University student Mahmoud Khalil , who had been released on bail in June last year after spending more than 100 days in ICE detention.

In January, the Third US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that lower federal district courts lacked subject matter jurisdiction to hear immigration or detention challenges while active removal proceedings are ongoing. While the order did not influence the core First Amendment arguments in Khalil’s case, it stripped away crucial procedural safeguards.

articles.title: Deadly helicopter crash kills 2 pilots battling raging wildfire in Yosemite
articles.summary: The FAA and NTSB are investigating the Precision Helicopters crash that killed two pilots battling the Dome Fire wildfire in Yosemite National Park. So far, the cause of the crash is a mystery.
articles.body: Two pilots were killed when a firefighting helicopter crashed while battling a wildfire in Yosemite National Park. The helicopter went down while conducting water bucket drops on the Dome Fire on Sunday, according to The Associated Press (AP). The pilots were the only people aboard the aircraft. They worked for Precision Helicopters, a company contracted to support the firefighting operation, the AP reported. 'WE THOUGHT WE WOULD DIE': PASSENGERS THROWN INTO CEILING DURING TERRIFYING FLIGHT The deceased pilots were later identified as Ryan Cutter and Greg King, according to social media posts from Precision Helicopters. Cutter had been a helicopter pilot since 2011, including a year-and-a-half with Precision Helicopters, according to his LinkedIn profile. He was described as a "deeply loved husband, son, friend and godfather" on GoFundMe. King had previously worked on wildland fires in Alaska and extensively alongside the Alaska Division of Forestry & Fire Protection, according to a statement from the agency. The agency said King had close ties to its wildland firefighting community, including loved ones who currently work for the division. "Greg was a dedicated aviator and a dear friend to many of us," the agency said. "We are mourning both pilots who bravely supported firefighting efforts, and our hearts go out to their families." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Precision Helicopters also paid tribute to Cutter and King in a social media post following the crash. "These two men brought honor to the mission. Their dedication and service will never be forgotten," the company wrote. The Super Puma helicopter was using a water bucket to help suppress the Dome Fire when it crashed near a lake, Benjamin Cossel, a spokesperson for the Federal Complex Incident Management Team overseeing the firefighting response, told AP. The FAA and National Transportation Safety Board will investigate the crash, with the NTSB leading the investigation, according to the FAA. Hundreds of firefighters are continuing to try to contain the Dome Fire. The crash occurred as hundreds of firefighters continued working to contain the Dome Fire, which started on Sept. 15 near Wawona, California. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ About 580 personnel were battling the wildfire, which had burned roughly 4.7 square miles and was about 15% contained, the AP reported. The crash site was southeast of Ostrander Lake, about seven miles northeast of Wawona and roughly nine miles south of Yosemite's El Capitan, according to the AP. A procession carrying the two deceased helicopter pilots was seen traveling through Merced on Monday, Sept. 21, according to Fox 26 in California. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Writing on Facebook about the somber procession shown on video, one user said, "Prayers for their families and loved ones. May they rest in peace." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Another said, "They paid the ultimate price for all of us. May God bless their families." The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: Concern grows for North Carolina woman who vanished during extreme June heatwave
articles.summary: Dana Ammons was last seen on security footage walking along U.S. 70 between Havelock and New Bern, North Carolina, on June 22, 2026. The Havelock Police Department is investigating her disappearance.
articles.body: Fifty-year-old Dana Ammons loves the beach. That’s why she moved to Havelock, North Carolina, just half an hour from her favorite spot: Atlantic Beach. “She wanted to be near the beach,” daughter Katelyn Lane told Dateline. Katelyn lives about an eight-hour drive away in western North Carolina, near the Tennessee border. She says her mom liked living in Havelock, but was “really isolated” because she had no family nearby. “She was living in a duplex by herself,” Katelyn said. “She had a hard time making friends, ‘cause she was shy.” Katelyn tried to encourage her mother to join social groups and try new hobbies to meet new people. “She’s always been really sweet and kind,” Katelyn said. “She’s just a great person. She just -- she struggles with her mental health.” Katelyn describes her mother as having “auditory and visual schizophrenia,” and says Dana experienced a lot of change in April: She got a new medical care team, quit her job, and stopped taking her medication. In May, Dana asked Katelyn to start using Life360, an app designed to help families keep track of one another to stay safe. “We had it before, but she was really nosy, so she would always, like, watch my every move and then get onto me if I’m speeding or something,” Katelyn said. So Katelyn stopped using it. When her mom asked her to use the app again, Katelyn recalls her saying “that if she got lost, um, she would want somebody to be able to find her.” Just weeks later, Dana vanished. Piecing together what happened around the time of Dana’s disappearance has been complicated, as Chief Mike Broadwell of the Havelock Police Department told Dateline. “It’s a little complex,” he said. “This is a multi-jurisdictional case.” His department is working with the Craven County Sheriff’s Office and the North Carolina State Bureau of Investigation (SBI) on Dana’s case. Sergeant Anita Guerrero of the Havelock Police Department’s Criminal Investigations Division shared some key details via email. She wrote that on June 30, Dana’s care team went to the Havelock Police Department to report that they had not seen Dana since June 19. A Havelock patrol officer then “attempted to contact Dana at her residence and by phone but was unsuccessful,” Sgt. Guerrero wrote. “A BOLO (Be on the Lookout) was sent to all agencies within a 50-mile radius.” Chief Broadwell told Dateline there were no noticeable issues during the welfare check. “Nobody was home, um, nothing missing. No -- no signs of breaking and entering,” he said. According to Sgt. Guerrero, on June 30, a Craven County Sheriff’s Office deputy informed Havelock PD that deputies had responded to a dealership “regarding a female subject matching Dana’s description who walked away and left her vehicle at the business” on June 22. Authorities learned Dana went to the Riverside Chrysler dealership located between Havelock and New Bern, along U.S. 70. “Dana gets out at this car lot and starts talking to one of the car lot folks about looking at a truck,” Chief Broadwell told Dateline. “She started acting a little strange.” The car salesman “said that she got a little agitated,” Katelyn told Dateline. “She was childlike, confused, and disoriented.” Katelyn says she learned her mother went into the woods next to the dealership for a little bit, and when she came out of the woods, she “ran blindly towards the busy highway.” “She left her car there with the keys in it and everything, and all her belongings,” Chief Broadwell said. “So we now have her car, we have her keys, we have her wallet.” Katelyn says Dana left the dealership around 10:30 a.m. At some point, she crossed the highway. “Between 10:37 and 10:40, she appeared down the road walking against traffic.” In a press release, Havelock PD stated that Dana “was last seen on video surveillance on June 22, 2026, at approximately 10:37 a.m. on foot near Caballus Trailers LLC (4605 U.S. 70), located between Havelock and New Bern, N.C.” She was traveling in the direction of New Bern. The press release also noted concern for Dana’s safety because of the extreme weather conditions at the time of her disappearance. “It was 105 heat index every day,” Broadwell told Dateline. “Ammons is believed to be traveling on foot in hazardous weather, raising significant concern for her safety,” the release continued. “Due to the severe weather and the potential risk it poses, locating her as quickly as possible is a priority.” “She gets seen on camera walking down that highway,” Broadwell said. “Not seen picked up. She’s not in distress. She just, uh, walked away.” “After that, we have no idea,” Katelyn told Dateline. That surveillance footage contains the last known images of Dana Ammons. She was wearing a white T-shirt and black jogger athletic pants with a white stripe down each leg, and white shoes. Sergeant Guerrero said in an email that the “dealership stated they called the Craven County Sheriff’s Office at approximately 2:00 p.m.” Dateline reached out to the Craven County Sheriff’s Office to ask about the steps they took after they got the call, but has not heard back. “We did interview the folks from the car lot, and we interviewed all the local businesses,” Chief Broadwell said of his department. “Checked surveillance cameras in that area, and did a -- did a lot of legwork down there.” On July 2, Dana was officially reported missing by her son-in-law, Katelyn’s husband. Havelock PD entered Dana into the FBI’s National Crime Information Center database as an ‘Endangered Missing Person’ and issued an updated BOLO. Dana was also entered into the North Carolina Center for Missing Persons database at that time. “I was just kind of in shock for a little bit,” Katelyn told Dateline. Then she remembered about the Life360 app they’d started using again in May. “I was like, ‘I’m gonna go on there and see where she was last.’” According to Katelyn, Life360 showed Dana’s location history was last updated on June 19, three days before she was seen at the dealership. “I don’t know if her phone died or if she turned off location permissions,” Katelyn said. She wasn’t sure her mom could have done that, though, as she often struggles with technology. “She didn’t really know how to do stuff like that.” According to Sgt. Guerrero’s email, on July 4, “Havelock Investigators executed a search warrant on Dana’s residence,” and her cell phone was located. Katelyn says she and her husband headed to Havelock to look for Dana as soon as they could. “We tried to retrace her steps,” she said. They looked at campgrounds, homeless encampments, and shelters. “We didn’t have any luck.” They also checked Dana’s favorite spot: Atlantic Beach. “Which would’ve been way too far for her to walk, but we -- we searched anyway,” Katelyn said. “We drove from one end of the island to the other.” Chief Broadwell told Dateline his department has not conducted a ground search of the woods along U.S. 70 for Dana. “We got thousands and thousands of acres of woods here,” he said. “We would do ground searches if we have a reason to believe she’s in a certain area.” Havelock PD did go door-to-door in Dana’s neighborhood. “We did a search warrant on her house. We’ve done search warrants on her phone. We have reviewed the private security camera of her house,” Broadwell explained. “We depend a lot on digital footprint. We depend a lot on, um, banking records and, uh, you know, social media posts and -- and different, uh, associations of -- of friends, families, boyfriends, girlfriends, that kind of stuff,” Broadwell said. “This individual did not have a huge network of any of those, so she’s not an easy person to find.” “All of our normal investigative tools that we -- that we’re using are hitting dead ends right now,” the chief said. He thinks it’s possible Dana left on her own. “It’s still dangerous, you know, for anybody to leave home, um, and not tell anybody where they’re going. With any type of medical history, during, you know, extreme heat is not a good idea,” he said. “There is no evidence at all in this case to -- that would lead us to believe that there’s any foul play.” Katelyn does not believe her mother intentionally disappeared, and after three months with no communication, she fears the worst. She says she’s run through many scenarios: Was Dana scared and running from something? Could she have been picked up along the highway? Did she maybe get hurt out there in the woods? “I don’t think she had the mental capacity to take care of herself,” she said. At this point, Katelyn’s only hope is that more attention on her mom’s case will help bring her home. “I’m hoping that just more people see it and know about it,” she said. “I just wanna find my mom.” Dana is about 5’4” and 190 lbs., with shoulder-length gray-ish hair and brown eyes. She has a butterfly tattoo on her right shoulder and angel wings on her back. Chief Broadwell of the Havelock Police Department told Dateline his office is following up on every lead they receive; they just “don’t have a lot to go on right now.” They encourage anyone with information, no matter how small, to come forward. You can call the Havelock PD at 252-447-3212 or leave an anonymous tip online. If you have a story to share with Dateline, please submit it here.

articles.title: Dolly Parton free book scheme to expand in London
articles.summary: The late singer's Imagination Library posts children a free book every month until they turn five.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton's Imagination Library, which posts children a free book every month until their fifth birthday, is to double the number of London boroughs it covers.

The scheme, which runs in five boroughs, will expand to 10 boroughs.

It comes a month after the country singer died at the age of 80. She set up the library in 1995 in tribute to her father, who could not read or write.

Funded by the Postcode Lottery, the expansion of the scheme will make 157,000 children eligible.

Harriet Sedrick-Ugo, from south London, said the monthly books had given her four-year-old daughter Sienna "a lot more confidence".

"We read together every day and that's been made possible because we get a book once a month," she said.

"She loves reading for pleasure because we have so many books at home from the Imagination Library."

Sedrick-Ugo, an early years educator, said the expansion would take pressure off families.

"Buying books can be quite expensive, so if they're going to be getting it for free, that would be something a lot of families can benefit from," she said.

She added: "I think it's the kindest initiative ever and we are so very grateful to have something so meaningful gifted to us."

The scheme is universal, meaning every child in a participating area can sign up regardless of their family's income.

The Dollywood Foundation says more than seven million books have been delivered to children in the UK.

Jeff Conyers, president of the Dollywood Foundation, said Parton would have been "incredibly proud" to see it grow in the capital.

"Dolly always wanted the Imagination Library to be something that lived on for generations into the future," he said. "She was constantly pushing us about how we get the Imagination Library to more and more children and more and more families."

The announcement comes amid concern about how often young children are read to. Figures cited by the organisers suggest 41% of children aged four and under are read to frequently, down from 64% in 2012.

Teachers have also reported that 28% of children starting reception cannot use books properly, with some trying to swipe or tap the pages as if they were a screen.

Clara Govier, managing director of the Postcode Lottery, said: "Dolly understood the extraordinary power of something very simple: a child, a grown-up and a book."

The expansion is being marked with a celebration at the British Library ahead of Give Like Dolly Day on 25 September.
