articles.title: ESPN personality Chris Canty shares wildly inaccurate statement about Ole Miss football on 'First Take'
articles.summary: Chris Canty claimed Ole Miss had just two AP Top 10 wins in 60 years on "First Take," but the Rebels have 16 such wins since 2000 alone.
articles.body: With Week 3's showdown between LSU and Ole Miss delivering on every single level, talking heads were still reacting to the Rebels' 32-24 win over the Tigers on Tuesday morning. Given that it was one of the most highly anticipated college football games in recent history, taking a few days to dissect it all is well warranted, but if you're going to do so, you have to have the most basic facts correct. ESPN did not abide by that rule. 'First Take' host Stephen A. Smith was joined by former NFL players Jeff Saturday and Chris Canty to discuss Ole Miss quarterback Trinidad Chambliss and what his future in the league could look like. While Canty dropped compliment after compliment about Chambliss and his abilities, one statement he made about Ole Miss' history as a program was not even close to being accurate. "Ole Miss has had two wins against AP Top 10-ranked teams in the last 60 years, and that dude has both of them," Canty said while pointing to a graphic of Chambliss. While we can say that Canty is being a prisoner of the moment and also understand that he was likely fed that 'statistic' about the Rebels by a producer or researcher at ESPN, we can also recognize just how far detached from reality it is. MISSISSIPPI GOV TROLLS LANE KIFFIN, LSU AFTER OLE MISS DEFEATS TIGERS IN COACH'S RETURN TO OXFORD THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! As Canty noted, Chambliss led Ole Miss to a win over LSU on Saturday and against Georgia in last year's College Football Playoff, giving him two wins over AP Top 10 teams, but he and the program have accomplished that feat many, many more times than two. SIGN UP FOR THE DAILY OUTKICK NEWSLETTER Just last season, No. 4 LSU visited Ole Miss and Chambliss led the Rebels to a 24-19 win. In 2024, Jaxson Dart pushed the Rebels past No. 3 Georgia. Ten years earlier, Ole Miss beat No. 3 Alabama 23-17 and No. 4 Mississippi State six weeks later, before beating the Crimson Tide on the road the following year when Bama was the No. 2 team in the nation. Since the turn of the 21st century alone, Ole Miss has beaten 16 teams ranked inside the AP Top 10. Mistakes happen, but some are far more egregious than others, and Canty's certainly falls into that category.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia’s King Salman slams targeting of Mecca by ‘terrorist’ Houthis
articles.summary: Saudi monarch’s rare condemnation hints at sense of urgency in the kingdom amid ramped-up attacks from Yemen.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia’s King Salman bin Abdulaziz Al Saud has branded Yemen’s armed Houthi movement a “terrorist militia” and accused the Iran-allied group of repeatedly targeting the holy city of Mecca.

The 90-year-old Saudi monarch made the comments during a cabinet meeting on Tuesday, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) reported.

It was a rare sharp intervention in current affairs by the king, as most day-to-day affairs are led by his son, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

Deadly Houthi attacks this month have marked one of the greatest threats to Saudi Arabia’s security in years.

King Salman called the suspected Houthi targeting of the holy city a “heinous crime” and a provocation against Muslim sentiment worldwide, according to SPA.

Last week, Saudi Arabia said it had intercepted a drone launched by the Houthis towards Mecca , an accusation that the Houthis strongly denied, with Houthi leader Abdel-Malik al-Houthi calling the Saudi claims “a heinous lie”.

It was the first time in nearly 10 years that a security alert had been activated in Mecca, home to the Kaaba, Islam’s holiest site.

The Saudi monarch commended the military and security services for “defending the homeland and resolutely confronting any aggression against the holy sites, pilgrims, citizens and residents of the Kingdom”.

King Salman also cited a meeting between the crown prince and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in Cairo last week , as well as his conversations with French President Emmanuel Macron on “efforts to enhance regional stability and ensure the security and freedom of maritime navigation”.

Houthi missile and drone attacks increasingly target Saudi cities , energy infrastructure and shipping, opening another front in the wider regional conflict that began with the United States and Israel’s war on Iran in February.

On Saturday, Saudi-led coalition forces in Yemen said they had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards the Saudi capital Riyadh, sending a dark column of smoke from a fuel storage area at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The escalation has also raised the stakes for global energy supplies, as Houthi fighters expanded their control to Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast, which has been used as an alternative route for Saudi oil exports amid the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Amid growing regional tensions, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan last month signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, which treats an armed attack on any of its three member countries as an attack on all three.

articles.title: Alabama has cleared a $2.52 billion federal loan for its largest infrastructure project ever; the new Mobile River bridge aims to end a decades-old bottleneck and reroute hazmat trucks
articles.summary: US News: A $2.52 billion federal loan has been approved to build the Interstate 10 Mobile River Bridge and Bayway project, clearing the way for the largest inf.
articles.body: A $2.52 billion federal loan has been approved to build the Interstate 10 Mobile River Bridge and Bayway project, clearing the way for the largest infrastructure project in Alabama's history. US Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy announced the approval of the low-interest loan, which provides key funding for the $4.15 billion project aimed at fixing a decades-old traffic bottleneck along the Gulf Coast. The massive construction project will replace aging roads, widen Interstate 10, and build a high-clearance cable-stayed bridge over the Mobile River. Beyond easing traffic for interstate commuters and freight trucks, the new bridge will reroute hazardous materials away from the George Wallace Tunnel under the Mobile River, solving long-standing safety and environmental concerns in downtown Mobile.Breaking a decades-old Gulf Coast bottleneckInterstate 10 is a key freight route connecting the East and West coasts of the United States. In southern Alabama, the highway narrows to two lanes in each direction through the George Wallace Tunnel, causing daily traffic jams that stretch for miles during busy travel hours and holidays. According to technical figures published by the Alabama Department of Transportation (ALDOT), the current infrastructure was built in the 1970s to handle around 35,000 vehicles a day. Today, traffic often tops 80,000 vehicles daily, far beyond what it was built for. The new cable-stayed bridge will offer six lanes across the Mobile River with a vertical clearance of more than 215 feet, allowing large container ships and oil tankers to pass freely to and from the Port of Mobile. Along with the river crossing, the project includes replacing and widening the existing low-lying Bayway bridges across Mobile Bay, building a raised structure above 100-year storm surge levels.Rerouting hazardous materials away from urban centersFederal safety rules currently ban vehicles carrying hazardous, flammable, or toxic materials from entering the Wallace Tunnel beneath the Mobile River. Because of this, chemical tankers and hazmat trucks must detour through downtown Mobile streets and residential neighborhoods before crossing the river via the Bankhead Tunnel or the Cochrane-Africatown USA Bridge. Official project details released by ALDOT confirm that the new Mobile River Bridge will offer a direct, designated route across the river for commercial hazmat traffic. Moving heavy hazardous cargo onto the elevated interstate bypass takes dangerous materials off local streets, lowering safety risks for downtown residents and historic business districts.Funding structure and federal supportThe financing secured through the US Department of Transportation operates under the Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (TIFIA), which offers flexible repayment terms backed by future toll revenue. In an official statement released by the US Department of Transportation, Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy spoke about the strategic value of the federal backing. "President Trump vowed to get Alabama the infrastructure it deserves, and since assuming office, my department has worked diligently over the last 100 days to make it happen," Duffy said. "Now that the I-10 grant agreement is a done deal, the state can get shovels in the ground and start moving dirt." The federal loan adds to a previously awarded $550 million federal grant from the Federal Highway Administration's Bridge Investment Program, along with state infrastructure bonds.Toll rates and commuter protectionsTo repay the construction costs, the new bridge and Bayway system will operate as a toll road once construction is finished. Official financing documents published by the Alabama Department of Transportation outline a tiered toll system built around the state's ALGOpass electronic transponder system. Local commuters will have access to an unlimited monthly pass capped at $60, which state officials have locked against annual toll increases for the first ten years of operation. Individual passenger vehicle trips using the ALGOpass will start at $3.00, while vehicles using out-of-state transponders will pay $7.70 per crossing. Drivers using unregistered pay-by-plate billing will face a $15.40 charge per trip. ALDOT confirmed that existing non-interstate options, including the Causeway, the Bankhead Tunnel, and the Wallace Tunnel, will remain toll-free for local drivers looking for non-express routes. Construction management is led by the joint venture team Kiewit Massman Traylor. Main bridge construction is set to begin after final ground preparation, with full traffic opening currently expected in 2031.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump says he would back ban on diesel exports as pump prices hit record
articles.summary: Republicans lawmakers have put pressure on the president to curb exports as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said he would back proposals to halt American diesel exports in a bid to ease prices for drivers at the pumps.

His comments come after Republicans lawmakers put pressure on the president ahead of November's mid-term elections to curb exports, as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US.

Speaking on the sidelines at the United Nations General Assembly, Trump suggested keeping domestic supplies inside the US could also ease broader petrol prices.

"I've called for that too. I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline," he said .

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed officials were assessing "whether a full or partial ban would work" without disrupting refinery capabilities.

National average diesel prices surpassed $6.50 (£4.87) a gallon on Tuesday according to AAA data, a new high.

The conflict in the Middle East has constrained global oil supplies, putting pressure on pump prices.

The surge in the cost of diesel has sparked political urgency ahead of crucial mid-term elections on 3 November, with several Republicans pressing the administration to restrict the fuel's export to ease financial strain on voters.

US Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate in Iowa, said on Monday that the state's consumers were "being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump."

In Alaska on Tuesday, Senator Dan Sullivan similarly urged for a "temporary pause of American diesel and exports" to rebuild domestic reserves.

Adding to the global market volatility, Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy facilities has knocked out the country's refining capacity.

"It is a serious hit on the Russians," Trump said during a meeting with Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. "It's also a serious hit on the price of diesel."

Trump confirmed he would discuss the strikes with the Ukrainian president, alongside broader efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict. "I think it's going to happen," he said.

Kyiv has intensified drone attacks on Russian processing plants in recent months to choke off the Kremlin's primary source of war funding.

Because Russia ranks among the world's leading diesel suppliers, reduced refining capacity – combined with Moscow's own strict export bans – has severely squeezed global reserves.

While restricting US exports could offer short-term relief for American drivers, a ban may risk pushing up prices internationally.

The US exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel per day – nearly a quarter of its refining output.

Cutting these shipments could put pressure on supplies for Western allies, including the UK and the Netherlands, which have relied on American fuel to cover deficits left by sanctions on Russian energy.

articles.title: Why didn't Ryan Clark push back at Colin Kaepernick comparing the NFL to slavery during interview?
articles.summary: Colin Kaepernick doubled down on his NFL-slave trade comparison in a podcast interview with Ryan Clark, calling the NFL Combine a "meat market."
articles.body: Colin Kaepernick doubled down on his comparison of the NFL to the slave trade during a podcast interview with former ESPN commentator Ryan Clark this week. "When did you truly start to have the realization that [the combine] reminds [you] of the slave trade?" Clark asked. "You get to the point, where it's like, 'Strip down to your drawers,’" Kaepernick responded. "It feels like a meat market." 5 TOUGH QUESTIONS COLIN KAEPERNICK DIDN'T HEAR DURING HIS MEDIA TOUR | MATT CALKINS Kaepernick added that he did not have the "historical perspective at the time" in 2011 at the Scouting Combine to understand what he now considers a "parallel" to a slave auction. The former NFL quarterback first made the comparison during a 2021 Netflix series. His reputation has never been the same since. That is how offensive it is to equate the horrors of bondage with playing in the NFL for millions of dollars a year. But at this point, similar scrutiny must be applied to Clark. Consider the wording of Clark's question. He did not challenge Kaepernick's premise or ask him to substantiate it. Instead, he led him toward the desired answer by asking "when" he realized the NFL draft process resembled slavery. COLIN KAEPERNICK IS STILL UPSET THAT HIS MOM WANTED HIM TO DATE TAYLOR SWIFT, A WHITE WOMAN Clark then nodded along as Kaepernick claimed that the draft and slave auctions are part of the "same process." OutKick asked Clark on Tuesday about his question to Kaepernick. We also asked whether he agreed with the analogy. Clark did not respond by the time of publication. We will update this story if he does. At minimum, it is reasonable to conclude that Clark did not find the comparison outrageous. We have seen how he reacts when he disagrees with a statement. Just ask ESPN host Peter Schrager, whom Clark continued to shout at behind the scenes after an on-air disagreement last year. On the merits, Kaepernick's analogy is indefensible. No serious person could reasonably equate the NFL draft process with an auction block. As the interviewer, Clark had a responsibility to identify the absurdity of the claim. He owed that to his audience. He did not live up to that responsibility. articles.body: Researchers have created the most detailed digital model yet of the Roman road network, mapping 299,171.31 kilometres, or roughly 186,000 miles, of roads across the empire's full territorial extent. Published in Nature Communications, the study ‘Network science reveals the structure and lasting impact of the Roman road system’ used network science to test long-held assumptions about Roman roads, whether they were truly straight, how central cities like Rome actually were, and how closely Roman infrastructure still lines up with modern roads today. Here's what the empire-wide analysis found.Mapping nearly 300,000 km of Roman roads across the empireThe research team mapped the road network of the Roman Empire at its territorial peak in 117 CE, when it stretched across almost 5,500,000 square kilometres around the Mediterranean. In total, they traced 299,171 kilometres of roads across a study area of just over 5.27 million square kilometres, working out to a density of about 57 metres of road for every square kilometre of land. Of all that road, roughly 91% (271,000 km) sat on gentle enough slopes for carts and wagons to actually use. Not every stretch was mapped with the same certainty, only about 3% of the roads are based on firm archaeological evidence, while the rest is either a well-informed guess (7%) or a reconstruction based on patterns and context rather than direct traces on the ground (90%).How straight were Roman roads really?The study found Roman roads had a mean sinuosity of 1.048, close to fully straight but consistently less so than modern roads, which measured 1.024 on average. Roads tended to be straightest in lowland regions such as Western Europe, the Pannonian basin, North Africa and central Anatolia, where topography allowed for more direct routes. Main roads, likely representing public and military routes, showed slightly lower sinuosity than secondary roads, closer to modern road standards. The researchers concluded that while Roman engineers consistently favoured straight alignments where terrain permitted, the long-held assumption that Roman roads were uniformly rectilinear across the empire doesn't hold up.Provincial capitals and Rome's centrality in the road networkResearchers ranked every city by how central it was to getting around the empire on foot or by cart, and found something surprising, 24 of the 45 provincial capitals landed among the best-connected places in the whole network, showing these cities weren't picked at random, they sat where the roads naturally converged. Byzantium came out especially well placed, since it was the bridge point where Europe's roads met Asia's, crossing over near the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. But here's the twist, despite the old saying that "all roads lead to Rome," Rome wasn't actually the best-connected city by land. Places like Antioch, Ankara, Byzantium and Corinth all beat it. Rome's real strength lay elsewhere, in how well it was connected by sea and river, not by road.What Roman roads reveal about modern infrastructureRoman roads and modern roads still tend to run in roughly the same places, the study found. But some regions have grown their roads a lot since Roman times, while others haven't. Northern Italy, the area around the Rhine and Meuse rivers, and Britain have all seen the sharpest jumps in road density since Roman times, especially around cities like Paris, Marseille and Madrid. Some of today's biggest cities, including Birmingham, Brussels, Paris and Madrid, grew from small Roman-era settlements into major metropolitan centres, which explains a lot of that growth. Meanwhile, Greece, Turkey, Tunisia and Algeria tell the opposite story. These were some of the busiest, most road-connected parts of the Roman Empire, but today they have comparatively few roads by comparison. So it's not that Rome built more roads where things are busy now; it's that some places kept building long after Rome, and others simply didn't.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
